title: How high is high? Using percentile thresholds to identify peak bat activity
abstract: Passive acoustic monitoring is a common tool used for monitoring bat activity levels. Identifying periods and locations of peak levels provides insight into bat ecology and has important management implications. One limitation of passive acoustic monitoring is the relative nature of the data, often relying on subjective interpretation of descriptive terminology such as “higher” or “lower”. We propose the use of percentile thresholds (PTs) for objectively identifying peak activity. By compiling a reference data set, it is possible to deﬁne percentiles of the observed activity levels and these percentiles can provide objective thresholds for comparing activity levels. We used acoustic recordings from sites in Canada and calculated PTs based on the distribution of the number of calls per hour across all nights and sites for three species of bat. Given species ecologies (e.g., hibernating, migrating), we were able to use PTs to objectively identify peak activity levels on a species-speciﬁc basis. Percentile thresholds are also a replicable method of describing within-night activity by evaluating species-speciﬁc activity patterns and important times of night. Our analyses and examples represent a proof of concept. The next step is to move towards a standardized distribution to generate PTs. Creating a public repository of acoustic data sets to evaluate activity of a species in the context of its entire range would allow us to standardize terms such as “high” activity in an objective manner.

## How high is high? Using percentile thresholds to identify peak bat activity

**Article** _in_ Canadian Journal of Zoology · March 2015

DOI: 10.1139/cjz-2014-0230

## **4 authors:**

## ARTICLE

## How high is high? Using percentile thresholds to identify peak bat activity

Amanda M. Adams, Liam P. McGuire, Lauren A. Hooton, and M. Brock Fenton

**Abstract:** Passive acoustic monitoring is a common tool used for monitoring bat activity levels. Identifying periods and locations of peak levels provides insight into bat ecology and has important management implications. One limitation of passive acoustic monitoring is the relative nature of the data, often relying on subjective interpretation of descriptive terminology such as “higher” or “lower”. We propose the use of percentile thresholds (PTs) for objectively identifying peak activity. By compiling a reference data set, it is possible to define percentiles of the observed activity levels and these percentiles can provide objective thresholds for comparing activity levels. We used acoustic recordings from sites in Canada and calculated PTs based on the distribution of the number of calls per hour across all nights and sites for three species of bat. Given species ecologies (e.g., hibernating, migrating), we were able to use PTs to objectively identify peak activity levels on a species-specific basis. Percentile thresholds are also a replicable method of describing within-night activity by evaluating species-specific activity patterns and important times of night. Our analyses and examples represent a proof of concept. The next step is to move towards a standardized distribution to generate PTs. Creating a public repository of acoustic data sets to evaluate activity of a species in the context of its entire range would allow us to standardize terms such as “high” activity in an objective manner.

_Key words:_ acoustic monitoring, activity levels, Chiroptera, thresholds, temporal variation, within-night variation.

## **Introduction**

Researchers passively monitor bats by eavesdropping on their echolocation calls (Hooper 1966). This approach provides insight into many aspects of ecology and behavior (e.g., Neuweiler 1989; Fenton 2003). Determining the timing and location of peak activity levels is important for an understanding of ecology and behavior of bats and these data have implications for management and conservation of bats.

Levels of bat activity often vary dramatically in space and in time. There is a tendency for increased activity during certain life-history events, such as prehibernation swarming (Fenton 1969; Parsons et al. 2003; Piksa 2008), or at ecologically relevant

sites, such as riparian foraging areas (Rautenbach et al. 1996; Hayes 1997), maternity colonies (e.g., Murray and Kurta 2004), and migration stopover sites (e.g., Barclay 1984; Dzal et al. 2009). Conversely, areas used by bats for commuting or dispersed foraging are likely to have lower levels of activity.

We know of no reliable way of translating the numbers of echolocation calls or bat passes recorded into the number of bats present. Individual bats may be detected repeatedly and thus the assumption of acoustic monitoring is that a greater number of calls or passes detected reflect a greater number of bats present. Acoustic monitoring only provides information about levels of bat activity, which can be compared to give relative indications of low

Previously, several methods have been used to identify peaks of activity, including visual identification with activity plots (Hayes 1997), choosing an arbitrary level of activity as “high” (Broders 2003; Brooks and Ford 2005), or calculating the number of calls above a certain threshold (Gorresen et al. 2008, 2009; Hamilton 2012). Since acoustic monitoring provides a relative indication of bat activity, it is important to define objective criteria for making comparisons among sites or time periods.

The potential importance of bats as bioindicators requires standardized approaches for the assessment of bat activity (Jones et al. 2009; Stahlschmidt and Brühl 2012). When monitoring bat activity, for example in areas where timber is being harvested or solar or wind power captured, conservationists and developers must present data on bat activity and put them in some broader context. Therefore, our specific goal was to determine a method for using percentile thresholds (PTs) to objectively identify peaks in bat activity.

Percentile thresholds have been used to identify high occupancy sites and make inferences about habitat attributes (Gorresen et al. 2008, 2009). Percentiles are simply 100 regular intervals in any cumulative distribution with the median at the 50th percentile where half of all observations fall below this threshold. Percentile thresholds are not affected when data differ in dispersion pattern and are less susceptible to outliers than traditional statistics (Sokal and Rohlf 1981). Ecological data are often overdispersed (O’Hara and Kotze 2010), with many observations with few calls and few observations with many calls, which violates key assumptions of common statistical methods. Thus, PTs may provide a more robust analytical framework for comparing activity levels. When applied to acoustic bat activity, the 99th percentile represents the most infrequently encountered levels of bat activity (those with the greatest number of calls), where these periods of high activity only occur 1% of the time.

To illustrate the use of PTs, we used acoustic recordings from several sites in Canada. The aims of this paper are ( _i_ ) to explore the suitability of PTs for identifying peak bat activity within and among nights and ( _ii_ ) to compare the use of PTs as a descriptive statistic to statistical analysis (mixed models).

## **Materials and methods**

## **Study areas**

Data were recorded at ( _i_ ) Long Point, Ontario, a 35 km long peninsula extending from the north shore of Lake Erie, for six nights during spring (June 2008) and six night during autumn migration (August–September 2008); ( _ii_ ) an abandoned mine near Renfrew, Ontario, for five nights during the early active season in spring (May–June 2008) and also autumn swarming (August 2008); and ( _iii_ ) along Battle Creek in Cypress Hills Interprovincial Park, Saskatchewan, for five nights during summer (July 2009).

We considered three species in our analysis: eastern red bat ( _Lasiurus borealis_ (Müller, 1776)), hoary bat ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ (Palisot de Beauvois, 1796)), and little brown bat ( _Myotis lucifugus_ (Le Conte, 1831)). Given the migratory nature of _L. borealis_ and _L. cinereus_ , we predicted that we would observe high activity in autumn at Long Point because it is an important site for bats during migratory periods (Dzal et al. 2009; McGuire et al. 2012). Cypress Hills is a forested region where all three species occur (Willis and Brigham 2003, 2005), although _L. borealis_ is rare (Willis and Brigham 2003) and we expected this site to be the least important to _L. borealis_ . _Myotis lucifugus_ is known to swarm and hibernate at Renfrew (Fenton 1969); therefore, we expected to observe high activity only during the swarming period.

## **Acoustic monitoring and analysis**

We standardized survey effort among all sites, recording continuously from dusk until dawn at all locations, on nights with no rain, using an externally polarized condenser microphone (Avisoft CM16/CMPA) connected to a real time, high-speed bat detector (Avisoft UltraSoundGate 416-200; Avisoft Bioacoustics, Berlin, Germany) with recording parameters set to 250 kHz sampling rate, 8 bit resolution, continuous recording, and gain set to a level of seven (as identified on the Avisoft recording hardware). The system was operated with Avisoft Recorder USG software. The microphone was positioned 1.5 m high and angled parallel to the ground at 90°. The same microphone was used among sites, but not calibrated between years.

We identified echolocation calls in all files using the automated detection feature in callViewer version 18 (Skowronski 2008; Skowronski and Fenton 2008), a custom sound analysis program written with MATLAB software (The MathWorks, Natick, Massachusetts, USA). We initially filtered the data to eliminate noise, terminal phase calls (feeding buzzes), and weak or fragmented calls, only including calls, regardless of species, with duration between 0.99 and 30 ms and a minimum frequency between 15 and 60 kHz. The filter parameters were selected based on conservative estimates of the echolocationcallstructureofthebatspeciespresentatourrecording sites. We identified calls to species using quadratic discriminant function analysis (DFA), which compared our unidentified data to a training data set that included seven species: big brown bat ( _Eptesicus fuscus_ (Palisot de Beauvois, 1796)), silver-haired bat ( _Lasionycteris noctivagans_ (Le Conte, 1831)), _L. borealis_ , _L. cinereus_ , _M. lucifugus_ , northern myotis ( _Myotis septentrionalis_ (Trouessart, 1897)), and tri-colored bat ( _Perimyotis subflavus_ (F. Cuvier, 1832)) (Adams 2013). To further improve classification accuracy and because DFA does not assign calls to an “unknown” category, we applied a post hoc, speciesspecific filter to remove any data that were above or below typical durations and minimum frequencies for each species (Adams 2013).

## **Statistical analysis**

The sampling unit in our analyses was the number of calls of a given species recorded each hour. We also summed the calls per hour of the seven species after DFA and filtering for the total number of calls per hour for all species combined (overall activity). We only included complete hours of recording starting at sunset. We calculated percentiles of activity using “quantile” in R version 3.0.1 (R Core Team 2014) for _L. borealis_ , _L. cinereus_ , _M. lucifugus_ , and overall activity based on the distribution of the number of calls per hour from the entire data set of all nights at all sites. We considered six percentiles (the 25th, 50th (median), 70th, 90th, 95th, and 99th percentiles) for each species and overall activity. The number of calls per hour at each percentile was the PT level.

A common challenge when dealing with acoustic monitoring data are the frequent absence of activity. Many time periods have no echolocation calls, reflected in the design of modern bat detectors that only record when triggered by echolocation calls. The abundance of time periods with no bat activity leads to serious issues of zero inflation in parametric statistical analysis (McCullagh and Nelder 1989). Zero inflation also creates challenges for the definition and interpretation of PTs. In cases with relatively few time periods containing echolocation calls, including all time periods in the definition of thresholds could lead to cases where, for example, the median could be zero calls. Such a distribution complicates the interpretation of activity levels, as any activity at all could be considered high (higher than the median). Thus, we excluded time periods when no bats were recorded from the distribution of activity used to generate the PTs. This approach frames our analysis in terms of ranking activity “given the presence of bats”. We recognize that the absence of activity is informative and differs from nondata, but our objective is to consider thresholds to be a method of providing context to the level of activity. By creating a large data set of recordings from a wide range of ecological situations, we created a null distribution to generate PTs. We then compared results from a particular site to the PTs of the larger distribution. We counted the number of nights with at least 1 h above each PT.

We also examined activity levels using generalized linear mixed models (GLMM). We compared activity levels and calls per hour including time periods with zero activity among sites and seasons with a GLMM fit by Laplace approximation and a Poisson distribution (“glmer” in lme4 package in R; Bolker et al. 2009; Bates et al. 2011). Data were not transformed to normality because transformations of count data can increase bias that is negligible when using an appropriate model, such as the Poisson distribution (O’Hara and Kotze 2010). The night of recording was included as a random effect, while season nested in site was included as a fixed effect. We tested for the significance of site and season on activity levels by comparing between models and selecting the model with the lower Akaike’s information criterion (AIC) score (“anova” in stats package in R; R Core Team 2014), and if site was significant, then we used Tukey’s post hoc test (“glht” in multcomp package in R; Hothorn et al. 2008). Like many ecological studies with count data, our data set was overdispersed (Richards 2008), where many hours contained few echolocation calls, resulting in greater variability than expected (variance > mean). We used additive overdispersion to account for overdispersion in our model by including an individual-level random effect, adding a random intercept with one level per observation that captures overdispersion (Elston et al. 2001; Browne et al. 2005).

To illustrate the potential for within-night comparisons, we used the previously calculated PTs to evaluate patterns of within-night activity for _L. borealis_ at Long Point and _M. lucifugus_ at Renfrew. We identified when peaks, defined as activity over the 50th PT, occurred, whether at dusk (first hour of the night), in the middle of the night, or at dawn (within 1 h of sunrise), looking for patterns of unimodal, bimodal, constant (within same PT for entire night), or irregular (different peaks among all nights) activity among all nights.

## **Within nights**

_Lasiurus borealis_ within-night activity at Long Point during spring was below the 50th percentile 75% ± 11% of the time, with peaks of activity above the 50th percentile during the fifth or sixth hour of the night (Fig. 1A). During migration, activity was consistently above the 50th percentile throughout the night. Activity peaked above the 70th percentile in the middle of the night and at dawn, demonstrating consistent within-night variation in activity levels (Fig. 1B).

_Myotis lucifugus_ had unimodal activity above the 95th percentile 4 h after sunset on every night during swarming at Renfrew (Fig. 1D) and activity was 74% ± 18% of the time above the median, all in the middle of the night lasting until dawn (Fig. 1D). During spring, there was no regular pattern of activity, except a unimodal peak over the 50th threshold in the middle of the night, but activity was below the 50th percentile 62% ± 67% of the time (Fig. 1C). The contrast between the two seasons (activity exceeding 95th percentile in autumn, but only 70th percentile in spring) highlights ( _i_ ) the importance of this site during the autumn swarming season and ( _ii_ ) the relative difference in seasonal activity levels. The within-night PT analysis indicates similar (but not identical) nightly activity patterns in both seasons, but that activity pattern contrasts sharply with, for example, the activity pattern observed for _L. borealis_ at Long Point during fall migration.

## **Discussion**

Percentile thresholds allowed us to identify peak levels of activity relative to a larger data set. The PT approach allowed us to take into account among-site and within-night variation of activity and could be applied across any temporal or spatial scale. It is worthwhile to establish a definition of “high” activity for a given scenario (e.g., Broders 2003), but this requires a clear definition of what criteria are used to determine these levels and identify peaks. The PT approach minimized the effect of subjectivity when making decisions based on relative data and enabled objective identification of sites with high bat activity. We have also shown that using PTs to define high activity is a replicable method of describing within-night activity patterns and important times of night. We defined peaks in nightly activity as levels of activity exceeding the 50th PT, but the actual definition of a peak could vary depending on the objectives of the study. The important point is that this definition is objective. These data facilitate interpretation of how a site is used by bats and its potential significance. Such interpretations are crucial for mitigation and management.

One application of PTs is to identify scenarios based on the highest PT activity levels exceeded. For example, during swarming at Renfrew, activity levels of _M. lucifugus_ regularly exceeding the 95th percentile. This species did not show levels of activity above the 70th percentile at any other site that we sampled (Table 3D). Very high levels of bat activity appear to identify situations or locations that are important to bats; the ones that they use heavily. This is comparable with the approach of the Important Bird Areas Program (IBA) of BirdLife International. Here, areas important to birds are identified based on areas with significant numbers of threatened, range-restricted, migratory, or congregatory species (BirdLife International 2008). By the same logic, locations with activity over the highest thresholds could be

defined as important bat areas, with the assumption that high acoustic activity relates to many bats flying past the microphone. In the context of this analysis, defining PTs based on the “global” distribution of all activity levels observed across situations is appropriate. The question being posed is which sites, times, or situations include the highest bat activity levels.

Due to nonindependence and overdispersion of acoustic data, traditional statistical methods, whether parametric (e.g., ANOVA) or nonparametric (e.g., Kruskal–Wallis), are frequently inappropriate for analysis of activity data. Nonindependence of data may require more complicated analysis, such as mixed models, especially for data susceptible to overdispersion. GLMM analysis identified pairwise differences in activity levels among sites and identified sites that exceeded the 95th percentile as having higher activity than sites that only exceeded lower percentiles. We might consider two theoretical sites: one with 25 mean calls/h and another with 50 calls/h. The second site had twice the activity as the first and the GLMM would detect this difference, but if we describe these sites in terms of the overall percentile distribution from all of our recording situations, it would be readily apparent that neither site exceeds the 50th PT. Describing the data in terms of percentiles provides an intuitive interpretation of the relative activity level. Even though one site has twice the activity of the other, neither would be considered “high” activity sites in most contexts. Percentile thresholds are an easy descriptive statistic to identify important sites, situations, and times of night, allowing us to evaluate skewed distributions while looking at a finer scale. Ultimately the most appropriate analysis method will be defined by the research question being addressed. In some cases, analysis of PTs may be sufficient or preferred, but we argue that even in cases where more complex statistical techniques are required for

the final analysis, PTs provided a valuable tool for data exploration and description of the data.

The flexibility of PTs is illustrated by the simplicity by which we could compare either species-specific activity patterns or overall combined activity levels. Similar approaches combining subsets of species could be useful for addressing questions regarding any number of functional questions where multiple species could be involved (e.g., foraging guilds, ecomorphology, life-history characteristics such as migration). However, when combining multiple species for PT analysis, it is important to consider the species-specific echolocation characteristics. An example of a potential pitfall is evident from our analysis of activity at Long Point during the migration season. Analysis of the overall levels of bat activity (all species combined) suggested that Long Point is not particularly important to bats in general. But, when data for individual species were considered, Long Point emerged as important for migratory species, especially _L. borealis_ and _L. cinereus_ (Table 3B). Due to species-specific echolocation characteristics, the importance for the migratory species was masked. Certainly relative species abundances will affect activity levels (more bats, more calls detected). But if we consider the Long

Point example, overall activity (Tables 1, 3A) was most influenced by _M. lucifugus_ because of the nature of its echolocation, namely, shorter call durations and interpulse intervals (Miller 2001) result in more calls per individual per unit time. Because species differ in detectability and call production rate, it is important to consider speciesspecific characteristics when comparing species (Miller 2001).

The unit of measure is an important consideration when defining the data to be used for the percentile distribution and data analysis. In our analysis we considered the number of calls detected per unit time, although in other studies bat passes have been used to describe bat activity (Fenton 1970, 2004). Recording many bats simultaneously flying in the same airspace poses an issue for methods previously used for analyzing bat activity. At lower levels of activity, passes represent a sequence of calls produced by one bat flying past the microphone. In practice, however, distinguishing among passes by different bats becomes difficult (if not impossible) when many bats share the airspace. We advocate the use of numbers of calls rather than numbers of passes. Individual calls havediscretestartandstoptimesanditispossibletounambiguously identify calls that overlap in both frequency and time with full spec-

trum recordings. Regardless of whether percentiles are defined based on passes or calls, there remains no documented method of translating activity levels to numbers of bats. Pseudoreplication will always be a potential issue with acoustic monitoring. However, our main goal in advocating the use of PTs is to move towards more objective analysis techniques and avoiding subjectivity. The number of calls is an objective metric, while the defining number of passes may introduce subjectivity when higher activity levels lead to overlapping passes produced by multiple bats.

We believe that PTs are a valuable standardized metric allowing assessment in a broader context of the activity of bats recorded in any situation. Percentile thresholds can be applied whether data are in the form of calls, passes, or an activity index as long as a broad database is used to establish the PTs. We encourage developing the largest possible database for calculating percentiles to generate the broader context. With an extensive “global” data set that encompasses all aspects of temporal and spatial variation, it is possible to objectively identify the periods of highest activity and to objectively compare among recording contexts. The availability of a global data set would also allow for definition of thresholds based on subsets of recording contexts (e.g., comparison among swarming sites or among managed forests). Given the context of a specific research question and experimental design, such as summer foraging habitat, the PT method could be used to calculate thresholds from a single context with a distribution of years, seasons, and locations. However, in many research and management contexts, interpretation of observed thresholds defined by the global data set could be a powerful tool. For example, the 99th PT is the highest activity level observed across all possible recording situations and this level will only be observed rarely. Thus, sites meeting this criterion should be afforded appropriate management and conservation consideration (analogous to the IBA program). The percentile approach can also be used to determine benchmarks, such as the percentile range that activity levels at maternity colonies or swarming sites always exceed. Land managers might also use the method to objectively rank bat activity among sites to prioritize investment of limited conservation and management resources within their jurisdiction. Percentile thresholds also have potential for studies of bat activity at sites proposed for commercial developments. For example, the principle behind conducting preconstruction surveys at proposed wind-energy sites is to assess potential risks of turbines to bats in an area (Kunz et al. 2007). Environmental consulting agencies are challenged to make recommendations about the placement of turbines to avoid areas with “high” levels of bat activity. The use of PTs provides an objective method to identify “high” or “low” levels of bat activity, making it possible to make data-based recommendations.

We have demonstrated how PTs can be used to objectively describe levels of bat activity. This approach depends entirely on the underlying distribution of activity levels used to define the thresholds. It is important to generate a distribution that spans as many situations, years, and seasons as possible, using data collected with standardized sampling efforts and techniques among sites, including the use of the same model of detector among sampling bouts (Adams et al. 2012). If the base distribution used to define the thresholds in insufficient or inappropriate, interpretation of the resulting data could be misinformed. For example, if PTs were defined only from our recordings of _M. lucifugus_ from Renfrew during swarming, no other site would be considered to have “high” activity. Increasing the number of sampling points contributing to the overall distribution of activity levels increases the power of this analysis. Our current analysis presents a “proof of concept”. The next step we envision is to move towards a global (encompassing all relevant temporal and spatial variations relevant to the study system) null distribution to generate PTs. Our ability to place any given survey in the broader context will continue to improve as the database increases to include more natural variation (i.e., seasonal, annual, geographic, meteorological).

This approach will be even more effective if including standardized survey methods to increase comparability (Stahlschmidt and Brühl 2012). While data sets for defining thresholds may be compiled by individual researchers, laboratories, institutions, agencies, or companies, ideally this database will come about through collaboration, using standardized sampling and analytical methods, such as is the goal of the North American Bat Monitoring Program (NABat; https://www.fort.usgs.gov/science-tasks/2457, accessed 19 February 2015). Applying PTs to a public repository of acoustic data sets would allow us to standardize statements about relative activity levels in an objective manner, evaluating activity of a species in the context of its entire range.
